title: AI Governance for Supervisors
summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to assess firms' AI governance, model and fairness risk, and to shape the authority's approach to AI supervision.
intro: This training programme equips supervisory staff to oversee the growing use of AI across the financial sector: assessing firms' governance, challenging model and fairness risk, and responding to AI-driven risks with confidence.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give supervisors a practical understanding of how AI and machine learning are built and used in financial services, and the analytical tools to assess whether firms govern them well. Participants leave able to probe firms' AI governance, model risk and customer outcomes, identify red flags and contribute to the authority's own approach to AI supervision.
sections.What It Covers: AI and machine learning foundations, governance and ethics, explainability and model risk, bias and fairness, AI in trading and operations, AI in advice and consumer services, AI vulnerabilities and failure modes, AI regulation and the financial perimeter, SupTech, and building the authority's approach to AI risk.
Intended Audience: Supervisors and inspectors responsible for overseeing AI use by regulated firms across all sectors
Risk, policy and technology specialists working on digital finance, model risk or innovation
Senior managers and heads of department shaping the authority's approach to AI supervision
Learning Objectives: Explain how AI and machine learning systems are developed, deployed and fail in financial services
Assess the adequacy of a firm's AI governance, accountability and oversight arrangements
Evaluate model risk, explainability, bias and fairness in AI-driven decisions
Challenge firms on AI risks in trading, operations, advice and consumer-facing services
Apply AI regulation and international standards to the financial regulatory perimeter
Design an institution-wide approach to AI supervision, including the authority's own use of SupTech
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about three hours each, grouped into four pathways and delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a technical briefing with case studies, red flags and supervisory question exercises, and pathways or individual modules can be selected or tailored to the authority's needs.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of financial supervision or risk assessment is helpful. No technical background in AI or data science is required.
Core Reading: FSB, The Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence (2024)
IOSCO, The Use of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning by Market Intermediaries and Asset Managers (2021)
NIST, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) (2023)
OECD, Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence (2019, revised 2024)

modules.title: Foundations of AI and Machine Learning
modules.summary: A grounding in how AI and machine learning systems are built, trained and deployed in financial services, how they differ from rules-based and statistical models, and why firms are adopting them.
objectives: Explain how machine learning models are developed, trained and deployed
Distinguish traditional statistical models, machine learning and generative AI
Identify the drivers and patterns of AI adoption across financial sectors
syllabus: Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning in financial applications
The AI lifecycle: data, training, validation, deployment and monitoring
Generative AI and large language models: capabilities and limits
In-house build versus vendor AI: supervisory implications

modules.title: AI Governance Frameworks and Ethics
modules.summary: How firms should govern the design, deployment and use of AI, the ethical principles governance must address, and how supervisors assess a firm's governance maturity.
objectives: Explain the core components of an effective AI governance framework
Assess how accountability for AI-driven decisions is allocated within a firm
Evaluate a firm's AI governance against supervisory expectations
syllabus: Board and senior management accountability for AI systems
AI policies, risk appetite statements and model inventories
Ethical principles in practice: fairness, transparency and human oversight
The three lines of defence and model validation applied to AI

modules.title: Explainability, Transparency and Model Risk
modules.summary: Why complex AI models are hard to interpret, what explainability techniques can realistically deliver, and how model risk management should extend to machine learning and generative AI.
objectives: Explain the trade-off between model complexity and explainability
Apply model risk management principles to AI and machine learning
Evaluate a firm's model documentation, validation and monitoring
syllabus: Black-box models and interpretation techniques, from feature importance to counterfactuals
Explainability expectations by use case, from credit decisions to trading
Extending model risk frameworks to machine learning and generative AI
Supervisory questions on drift, retraining and independent validation

modules.title: Bias, Fairness and Discrimination
modules.summary: How bias enters AI systems and produces unfair customer outcomes, how fairness is measured and tested, and the supervisory tools for assessing fairness in AI-driven products and services.
objectives: Explain the sources of bias in data, model design and deployment
Analyse the fair-treatment and non-discrimination implications of AI decisions
Evaluate a firm's bias testing and fairness monitoring
syllabus: Historical data bias, proxy discrimination and feedback loops
Fairness metrics and their trade-offs in credit scoring and insurance pricing
Bias testing methodologies and ongoing outcome monitoring
Case studies: AI bias, supervisory findings and remediation

modules.title: AI in Trading, Investment and Operations
modules.summary: The use of AI in trading, investment management and back-office processing, and the supervisory risks that arise when AI systems act on markets and infrastructure at speed and scale.
objectives: Explain how AI is used in trading, portfolio construction and operations
Analyse the market integrity risks of AI-driven trading
Evaluate controls over AI systems operating with limited human intervention
syllabus: AI in algorithmic and high-frequency trading strategies
Portfolio construction, signal generation and AI-driven risk tools
Correlated behaviour, flash events and unintended algorithmic collusion
Kill-switches, human oversight and escalation for autonomous systems

modules.title: AI in Advice and Consumer-Facing Services
modules.summary: The growing use of AI in robo-advice, chatbots, personalisation and pricing, and the suitability, disclosure and fair-treatment questions supervisors should put to firms.
objectives: Explain how AI is used in digital advice and customer engagement
Assess the suitability and disclosure implications of AI-driven recommendations
Evaluate consumer protection risks from personalisation and automated advice
syllabus: Robo-advice and automated portfolio recommendation engines
Chatbots and virtual assistants: accuracy, complaints and vulnerable customers
Personalisation and dynamic pricing: fair-treatment implications
The guidance versus regulated advice boundary in AI-driven journeys

modules.title: AI Vulnerabilities and Failure Modes
modules.summary: A practical framework for identifying how AI systems fail, are manipulated or behave unexpectedly, and the evidence supervisors should request to test a firm's resilience.
objectives: Identify common AI vulnerabilities and failure modes
Analyse the operational, cyber and third-party risks specific to AI
Apply a structured framework to probe firms on AI resilience
syllabus: Drift, data degradation and silent failure in production systems
Adversarial attacks, data poisoning and prompt injection
Vendor dependency and sector-wide concentration on AI providers
Supervisory questions and evidence requests on AI resilience

modules.title: AI Regulation and the Financial Regulatory Perimeter
modules.summary: How jurisdictions are regulating AI, how horizontal AI rules interact with existing financial services requirements, and what overlapping regimes mean for supervisory practice and coordination.
objectives: Explain the main models of AI regulation and the obligations they create
Analyse how AI rules overlay conduct, prudential and consumer protection requirements
Evaluate coordination and perimeter issues between financial supervisors and other authorities
syllabus: Approaches to AI regulation: risk-based laws, sectoral rules and supervisory guidance
International standards and frameworks: OECD, NIST, ISO/IEC 42001, FSB, IOSCO and BIS
High-risk financial use cases and existing sectoral obligations
Coordination with data protection, competition and AI-specific authorities

modules.title: SupTech: AI in Supervisory Practice
modules.summary: How supervisory authorities can use AI and data analytics in their own work, drawing on SupTech and RegTech case studies, and the governance and resourcing constraints they face.
objectives: Explain how RegTech and SupTech tools support compliance and supervision
Analyse case studies of AI-enabled supervisory tools in practice
Evaluate the opportunities and limits of AI adoption within the authority
syllabus: RegTech used by firms for compliance monitoring and reporting
SupTech applications, including natural language processing of returns
Anomaly detection, network analysis and risk dashboards
Data quality, governance, skills and resourcing for supervisory AI

modules.title: Building the Authority's Approach to AI Supervision
modules.summary: Brings the programme together into a strategic view of how the authority should supervise AI risk, balancing innovation against conduct, prudential and systemic risk, and building lasting capability.
objectives: Explain the strategic choices facing authorities as AI adoption accelerates
Compare international approaches and coordination initiatives on AI in finance
Design options for AI supervisory capability, policy and resourcing
syllabus: International coordination on AI: FSB, IOSCO and BIS workstreams
Embedding AI oversight across existing supervisory functions
Generative AI and autonomous agents: emerging supervisory questions
Workshop: the authority's AI supervision roadmap

related.title: Agentic Finance for Supervisors
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to understand and supervise AI agents that transact and make financial decisions, from agent identity to payments and liability.

related.title: The EU AI Act and Financial Services (EU Edition)
related.summary: An eight-module programme on the EU AI Act for supervisors and financial firms: risk classification, high-risk credit and insurance uses, provider and deployer duties, supervision and compliance programmes.

related.title: SupTech, Data and Supervisory Analytics
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors and leaders to govern supervisory data, interrogate returns, use analytics to surface risk and build the authority's SupTech capability.

related.title: Applied AI for Supervisory Staff
related.summary: An eight-module hands-on programme helping supervisory staff use generative AI and analytics tools safely and productively in everyday supervisory work.

related.title: Financial Crime Supervision in the Age of AI
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to assess financial crime controls and firms' use of AI in monitoring, screening, fraud and surveillance.

related.title: FinTech Business Models: Understanding and Supervising Innovation
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors and firm compliance teams to understand how FinTech business models make money, grow and fail, and to assess their risks.
